source.title: Exploring Multimodal Perception in Large Language Models Through Perceptual Strength Ratings
source.authors: Jonghyun Lee; Dojun Park; Jiwoo Lee; Hoekeon Choi; Sungeun Lee

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the paper’s sections and references, but the contents of referenced tables are missing from the extraction. The prose reports the results recorded below.
record.tranche_reason: It compares model size with performance on a downstream perceptual-rating task, providing a conceptual test of downstream performance scaling. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper compares model sizes on perceptual-strength ratings, which bears on V6. It does not test held-out cross-entropy loss, token or compute scaling, extrapolation from small runs, compute-optimal allocations, or fixed-parameter architecture effects. Its comparisons of multimodality and model generation are not results on the scaling claim. Kaplan et al. is cited, but their loss-scaling results are not tested.
record.test_reason: Compares downstream alignment with human perceptual-strength ratings across sizes within four families (GPT, Gemini, LLaMA, Qwen). That bears weakly on V6 in a new task setting. There is no controlled scaling: models differ in training data and post-training, some sizes are undisclosed, and no curve is fitted. It does not test pretraining loss or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find larger models generally align better with human perceptual-strength ratings (6 of 8 comparisons). The relation is not linear and can diminish or reverse when size gaps are small. Their main conclusions concern grounding and multimodality, not scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates model outputs on perceptual-strength ratings and compares performance across existing model sizes; it does not train models across controlled parameter, token, or compute sweeps or fit held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The size trend varies by model family and evaluation metric: the paper reports exceptions for Gemini average correlation and Qwen cosine distance.

fits_no_version.finding: MoE models: LLaMA-4-Maverick and Qwen-3-30B-A3B perform near their total-parameter peers. LLaMA-4-Scout (109B total) and Qwen-3-235B-A22B underperform their total parameter counts. Authors say success depends on expert configuration rather than simple parameter scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance of MoE models tracks total parameters only for some expert configurations.

record.problems: The evidence concerns one downstream rating task and heterogeneous existing models, rather than controlled training runs or held-out pretraining loss. The supplied extraction omits table contents, and no uncertainty estimates are stated for the size-comparison percentages or the two named exceptions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-claim results were available to record. Comparisons of multimodality and architectural generation were omitted because they do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law form in other modalities or regimes. Multimodal vs text-only comparisons are not scaling fits.
Predictability from pretraining loss or from a fitted scale curve. Only pairwise size comparisons of uncontrolled released models are reported.
Dependence of exponents or allocations on setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Overall-metric size comparison result: larger models better in 6 of 8 within-family comparisons. This is distinct from the 62.5% modality-specific rate.
GPT and LLaMA families show consistent larger-model advantages across all sensory modalities. Advantage is strongest in gustatory, haptic and olfactory, weakest in vision.
Authors state the size–performance relation is not linear. Differences diminish or reverse when parameter counts are similar (Qwen-2.5, Gemini-2.5).

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is weak. It rests on pairwise comparisons of released models that differ in data, training and post-training, and some have undisclosed sizes. Table contents are absent from the text; full results are at OSF.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted to smaller runs.
Loss-minimizing parameter and token allocations at fixed compute, and their scaling with compute.
Held-out loss comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares size with one downstream rating task; it does not test prediction from pretraining loss or establish a fitted scaling relationship.
Dependence of loss-scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup or fitting choices, and departures from fitted power laws.

rows.measure: Comparisons in which the larger model showed better performance
rows.baseline: Smaller model in each within-family comparison
rows.value: Larger models showed better performance in 62.5% of comparisons.
rows.note: Aggregate comparison rate as reported by the authors; this is a downstream rating task, not a held-out loss scaling sweep.
rows.check: 62.5% is the modality-specific correlation comparison rate (Table 3). The overall-metric comparison is separately reported as 6 of 8 in the abstract, so the two should be distinguished. Subject is aggregate across families, and pairs are confounded by training differences. Table contents are missing from the text.

rows.subject: Gemini-2.5-Flash
rows.operation_detail: Compared perceptual-strength rating performance with a larger model in the same family.
rows.value: Gemini-2.5-Flash outperformed Gemini-2.5-Pro on average correlation.
rows.note: The paper identifies this as an exception to the general advantage for larger models.
rows.check: Parameter counts for Gemini-2.5-Flash and Pro are not disclosed. The 'larger' baseline is the paper's assumption, not a stated size. The reversal holds on average correlation only.
